source: Samani and Pan (2021) Interleaved practice enhances memory and problem-solving ability in undergraduate physics
finding: Preregistered classroom test. Interleaved homework was harder and felt worse, yet won on surprise tests. Students did worse on interleaved homework and rated it as teaching less.
numbers: Two lecture sections, about 290 students per stage. Homework accuracy blocked vs interleaved: stage 1 0.74 vs 0.69, stage 2 0.76 vs 0.67. Judgment of learning 'well' share: 0.57 vs 0.51 and 0.48 vs 0.40. Surprise criterial test: interleaving d = 0.40 (CI 0.17-0.65) stage 1; d = 0.91 (CI 0.66-1.20) stage 2. Median improvement 50% and 125%.
limits: Single course. Interleaved sets had 9 problem types against 3 in blocked sets, so interleaving and spacing are mixed. Midterms 3 days later showed no difference.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that practice-time accuracy points the wrong way. A scaffold that scores a lesson or strategy on its immediate pass rate would reject the better one.

source: Samani and Pan (2021) same paper: high-stakes exams
finding: A cramming-prone outcome measure hid the interleaving benefit. The real test of learning needed a delayed, surprise, novel-problem test.
numbers: Midterm 3 days after criterial test: stage 1 d = 0.20 (95% CI -0.04 to 0.43, p = 0.094); stage 2 d = 0.02 (CI -0.21 to 0.25, p = 0.876). Exit surveys: most students crammed before midterms but not before criterial tests.
limits: Authors explain the null by cramming. This is a post-hoc reading.
agent_relevance: Choose the evaluation probe carefully. A probe that short-term effort can game will wash out real differences.

source: Sigayret, Parmentier and Silvestre (2026) Testing the testing effect on Prolific: when retrieval practice fails to boost learning
finding: Two experiments on a crowd platform found no testing effect against restudy, despite feedback, delayed test and attention checks.
numbers: Exp 1: 67 of 120 completers (39.6%) came back for phase 2. Total score F(1,66) = 0.13, p = 0.72. Expressionism control 8.68 vs test 8.88; Rome control 10.83 vs test 10.47 (out of 20). Exp 2: 129 of 426 completed (30.3%); Mann-Whitney U = 1773, p = 0.17, r = 0.14.
limits: Not designed as direct replications. Heavy attrition, short real session times (about 14 min against 25 planned). Authors blame the sample, not the effect. Cells of 29-38.
agent_relevance: Desirable difficulty needs real effort to pay off. If the model gives a cheap answer to a retrieval or self-test step, the benefit may vanish. Measure whether the effortful step was actually done.

source: Sigayret et al. (2026) literature summary of testing-effect meta-analyses (as cited in the paper)
finding: The paper lists the standard effect sizes of the testing effect from earlier meta-analyses.
numbers: Phelps 2012: d = 0.55 to 0.88. Rowland 2014: g = 0.50. Adesope 2017: g = 0.61 to 0.70. Pan and Rickard 2018: smaller transfer effects. Yang et al. 2021 classroom meta confirms effect across levels.
limits: Second-hand: values quoted from the paper, not checked against the originals. Effects larger in higher education and with feedback.
agent_relevance: Testing effect is medium sized, not huge. Expect gains of about half a standard deviation at best.

source: Text generation effect conceptual replication (2025) Does text generation improve learning from expository text?
finding: Seven experiments found no generation effect for sentence unscrambling in expository text. Four showed a learning disadvantage. Only the one experiment matching the old conditions (intentional learning, unlimited time, immediate test, between subjects) showed a benefit, and only on one measure.
numbers: 7 experiments, final samples from N = 40 (Exp 1) to 152 (Exp 6). Prompted recall: generation effect in 0 of 7, disadvantage in 4 of 7 (Exp 3, 4, 5, 7). Multiple-choice: effect in 1 of 7 (Exp 6); reading control better in Exp 5.
quote: text generation was a learning difficulty but not a desirable one
limits: Specific task: unscrambling sentences. Other generation tasks may behave differently.
agent_relevance: A difficulty is not desirable by default. Extra steps that make the model work harder (rewrite, unscramble, restate) must be tested against a plain control at equal tokens.

source: Text generation effect conceptual replication (2025) boundary conditions
finding: The authors varied four contextual factors and conclude the effect is fragile: it needs intentional learning, no time pressure and immediate testing.
numbers: Manipulated: intentional vs incidental learning; time limit yes/no; retention interval immediate, 30 min, 1 week; between vs within subjects. Disadvantage seen at immediate (Exp 3, 5), 30 min (Exp 4) and 1 week (Exp 7) tests.
limits: Cross-experiment comparison, not one factorial design. A close replication by Schindler et al. 2024 of McDaniel et al. 1986 did find the effect under the old conditions (as cited).
agent_relevance: Boundary conditions matter: time pressure removed the benefit. Our agent runs on token budgets, which act like time pressure.

source: Hattie and Donoghue (2016) Learning strategies: a synthesis and conceptual model
finding: Synthesis of meta-analyses. Spaced practice and practice testing have moderate effects. Interleaving has a small effect from one meta-analysis.
numbers: Table of effect sizes: spaced vs mass practice d = 0.60 (4 metas, 360 studies); practice testing d = 0.44 (10 metas, 674 studies); interleaved practice d = 0.21 (1 meta, 12 studies); giving or receiving feedback d = 0.71; time on task 0.54.
limits: Meta of metas, so overlap and quality are mixed. Interleaving figure rests on 12 studies and predates Brunmair and Richter 2019.
agent_relevance: Feedback (0.71) beats spacing and testing in these tables. Our guardrail on revising from real output (G2) matches the largest effect.

source: Hattie and Donoghue (2016) strategy timing
finding: The authors say strategies pay off at different phases. Memorising has little value at the acquisition phase. Spaced investment helps at the consolidation phase.
numbers: No single new number. Phase model: surface acquisition, consolidation, then deep learning.
limits: Conceptual model, not directly tested in the paper.
agent_relevance: Difficulty helps once something is encoded. Early on, make the lesson easy; add difficulty afterwards.

source: de Bruin (2023) Dealing with desirable difficulties: supporting students to accept, reduce, or silence effort
finding: Students choose desirable difficulties poorly because effort feels like poor learning. Teachers need to explain the paradox and change how students judge effort.
numbers: Describes the S2D2 framework (Start and Stick to Desirable Difficulties). No new data in this keynote paper.
limits: Keynote summary. Intervention advice rests on cited work.
agent_relevance: Models, like students, may prefer the fluent path. The program, not the model, should choose the difficult step.

source: Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted and Rohrer (2006) Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks
finding: The largest early meta-analysis of the spacing effect. The best gap between sessions grows with how long you must remember.
numbers: 839 assessments of distributed practice, 317 experiments, 184 articles.
limits: Abstract only read this session. Verbal recall tasks only; mostly lab with short retention intervals.
agent_relevance: Spacing optimum depends on the delay to use. For an agent, the delay is the number of steps or calls between learning and use.

source: Brunmair and Richter (2019) Similarity matters: a meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators
finding: Interleaving helps on average, but not everywhere. It helps with visual categories and maths; it hurts or does nothing for words and expository text.
numbers: 59 studies, 238 effect sizes, 158 samples. Overall Hedges g = 0.42. Paintings g = 0.67. Maths g = 0.34. Words g = -0.39 (blocking better). Text and tastes not significant.
limits: Abstract only read. Helps when categories are similar to each other and items within a category are dissimilar.
agent_relevance: Interleave only when categories are confusable. Do not interleave unrelated problem types and expect gains.

source: Rowland (2014) The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: a meta-analytic review of the testing effect
finding: Testing beats restudy. Recall tests help more than recognition tests, which supports an effort account.
numbers: Overall g = 0.50 (as cited in Sigayret et al. 2026; the abstract gives no number).
limits: Abstract only read. Authors find limited support for the semantic elaboration account.
agent_relevance: Produce-style steps (free recall) give more benefit than choosing among options.

source: Yang et al. (2021) Testing (quizzing) boosts classroom learning: a systematic and meta-analytic review
finding: Quizzing helps in real classrooms, with a medium effect.
numbers: 222 independent studies, 48,478 students. g = 0.499. Moderators: control condition type, test-format match, feedback, number of repeats, timing.
limits: Abstract only read. Quizzes with corrective feedback and matched formats gave bigger effects.
agent_relevance: Retrieval steps need feedback from a check, matching our rule to revise from real output.

source: Pan and Rickard (2018) Transfer of test-enhanced learning: meta-analytic review and synthesis
finding: Testing transfers to new contexts, but after bias correction the benefit often shrinks to near zero without the right moderators.
numbers: 122 experiments, 192 effect sizes, N = 10,382. d = 0.40 (CI 0.31-0.50) vs re-exposure control. Weakest to rearranged items and worked-example problems.
limits: Abstract only read. Strong moderators: response congruency, elaborated retrieval, initial test performance.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a self-test step to transfer to different problem forms unless it is elaborated and matched.

source: Chan, Meissner and Davis (2018) Retrieval potentiates new learning: a theoretical and meta-analytic review
finding: Testing can help or hurt later learning of new material. Factors decide which.
numbers: No effect size read from the abstract.
limits: Abstract only read. Four theory classes: resource, metacognitive, context, integration; metaregression favours integration.
agent_relevance: Retrieval can interfere with later learning if contexts clash. Watch for carry-over harm between tasks in one run.

source: Soderstrom and Bjork (2015) Learning versus performance: an integrative review
finding: Performance during practice is an unreliable index of learning. Conditions that raise performance can lower retention, and the reverse. People misread their practice performance as a guide to long-term learning.
numbers: Review; no pooled effect size in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Core caution for our loop: an immediate pass is not learning. Judge by delayed, transfer probes.

source: Kornell and Bjork (2008) Learning concepts and categories: is spacing the enemy of induction?
finding: Painting-style learning. Interleaving artists beat massing for induction, yet people rated massing as better, even after their own test showed the reverse.
numbers: Experiments 1a, 1b, 2 on artist classification of new paintings; numbers not read.
limits: Abstract only read. Visual categories, the strongest case for interleaving in the Brunmair meta.
agent_relevance: The learner's own rating (like a model's self-confidence) can invert the truth.

source: Yan, Bjork and Bjork (2016) On the difficulty of mending metacognitive illusions
finding: Belief that blocking is better survives being told otherwise. Only when the two schedules' results were shown separately did a majority change their mind.
numbers: Six experiments. Experiments 3-5 debiasing had 'only modest effects'; Experiment 6 (separated test results plus theory) moved a majority.
limits: Abstract only read. Three causes: fluency, prior beliefs, belief that one is unique as a learner.
agent_relevance: Telling a model 'spacing is better' in the prompt will not change what it prefers to do; the program must enforce it.

source: Kornell, Hays and Bjork (2009) Unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance subsequent learning
finding: Guessing before seeing the answer helped later learning, even when the guess was wrong.
numbers: Six experiments with fictional facts and weak-associate cues; correct guesses excluded.
limits: Abstract only read. Lab materials, short delays.
agent_relevance: A 'predict first, then check' step can help if feedback follows. Fits testing a guess against real output.

source: Russin, Pavlick and Frank (2025) The dynamic interplay between in-context and in-weight learning in humans and neural networks (PNAS 122:35)
finding: A metalearning network with in-context learning (ICL) and in-weight learning (IWL) reproduces human curriculum effects: blocking wins with rule-like structure, interleaving wins without it. GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 showed the blocking advantage in context.
numbers: Human data cited: blocking advantage d = 0.47 for rule-like categories, interleaving advantage d = 0.33 when no rule; compositional task 47/58 generalised blocked vs 36/60 interleaved. Both LLMs: curriculum main effect p < 10^-3; both poor on the rotated task (p < 10^-3).
limits: Small task (colour-animal pairs, 9 study examples). Two older LLMs, in-context only, no weight updates (authors say fine-tuning was too costly).
agent_relevance: For in-context examples of rule-governed tasks, put similar examples together (blocked). The human interleaving advantage came from weight learning, which a prompt-only agent does not do.

source: Russin et al. (2025) flexibility-retention trade-off
finding: More errors lead to more in-weight learning and better later retention. Limiting access to context examples hurts flexibility and helps retention. This mirrors the claim that struggle aids memory.
numbers: Figure 5: ablating attention to context examples raises errors and retention in the model; matches human results under higher working-memory load.
limits: Result is from a small network, not from the LLMs.
agent_relevance: Difficulty helps long-term (weights) but hurts the live run. A scaffold that only cares about the current run gains nothing from desirable difficulty.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: evidence from high school mathematics (PNAS)
finding: Field experiment, nearly 1000 students. GPT-4 access raised practice scores, but after access was removed GPT Base students were worse than controls. A guarded tutor removed the harm.
numbers: Practice (assisted): GPT Base +0.137, GPT Tutor +0.361 on a 0-1 scale, control mean 0.284, so +48% and +127%. Unassisted exam: GPT Base -0.054 (SE 0.022; 17% below control mean 0.321); GPT Tutor -0.004 (SE 0.013, null). Control SD 0.277; 2,848 observations.
limits: Randomised by classroom. One school, maths, GPT-4. Few heterogeneity effects.
agent_relevance: Strongest real-world case of performance misleading: assisted performance up 48-127%, true learning down or flat. An aided pass is not evidence of skill.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) perception mismatch
finding: Students did not notice the harm. GPT Base students did not think they learned less, and GPT Tutor students thought they did better though exam scores were flat.
numbers: Self-report: GPT Base no perceived reduction; GPT Tutor perceived significantly better despite exam coefficient -0.004.
limits: Self-report data; exact survey effect sizes are in the SI, not read.
agent_relevance: Self-assessment is not a reliable check on learning. Use external held-out tests (G3).

source: Kestin et al. (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning (Scientific Reports)
finding: Crossover RCT in physics: AI tutor lessons gave more learning in less time than in-class active learning, measured on a post-test right after the lesson.
numbers: Median post-score 4.5 (N = 142) AI vs 3.5 (N = 174) in-class; pre-test baseline 2.75 (N = 316); median learning gain over double; rank-sum z = -5.6, p < 10^-8. Two lessons in consecutive weeks, groups swapped.
limits: Immediate post-test only; no delayed test, so it cannot separate learning from performance. Authors also report higher engagement and motivation.
agent_relevance: Counterweight to Bastani: a well-designed tutor can help. But the outcome was immediate, the measure desirable-difficulty theory calls unreliable.

source: Critical-thinking paradox in generative-AI-integrated learning (Frontiers in Psychology, 2026)
finding: A conceptual paper uses desirable difficulties, levels of processing, cognitive load and offloading to say when AI output gains diverge from durable learning. It proposes a three-level framework and a 'cognitive debt' idea.
numbers: No new experiment. Defines episodic vs habitual offloading.
limits: Conceptual; the authors call it a testable interpretation, not a fact. Authors' names not recorded.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis source for when an agent should be made to work unaided. Treat as a hypothesis.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT: accumulation of cognitive debt when using an AI assistant for essay writing
finding: EEG study: LLM users had the weakest brain connectivity and lowest essay ownership. Those who went from LLM to brain-only showed reduced alpha and beta connectivity.
numbers: 54 participants in 3 groups (LLM, search, brain-only); 18 reassigned in session 4. No effect sizes in the abstract.
limits: Abstract page only. Small groups; preprint. 'Cognitive debt' is the authors' label.
agent_relevance: Suggestive only. Do not rely on it for design.

source: Xue et al. (2024) PACIT: unlocking the power of examples for better in-context instruction tuning (ACL Findings)
finding: Makes a model first judge whether an example is correct before answering. The authors say it is inspired by desirable difficulty.
numbers: Up to +9.16 ROUGE-L in-domain and +3.14 out-of-domain over in-context instruction tuning (ICIT).
limits: Abstract page only. ROUGE-L is an immediate surface metric; no delayed test; no check that difficulty is what drives the gain.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence for difficulty helping LLMs. A verify-the-example step is a cheap thing to test.

source: Campos (2021) Curriculum learning for language modeling
finding: Linguistically motivated curricula did not clearly beat standard training on GLUE.
numbers: No numbers read.
quote: we do not find compelling evidence that curriculum learning methods improve language model training
limits: Abstract page only. Small-scale pretraining.
agent_relevance: Ordering and difficulty schedules in training have not shown reliable gains.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2023) Scaling data-constrained language models
finding: Repeating training data up to about 4 epochs costs almost nothing against unique data. More repetition then loses value toward zero.
numbers: Up to 900B tokens, models up to 9B parameters, 400 runs. Up to 4 epochs gives negligible change in loss.
limits: Abstract page only. Pretraining loss, not retention or reasoning. This is repetition, not spacing.
agent_relevance: Weak LLM analogue: re-exposure has a limited useful range. Not a test of the human spacing effect.

source: Clegg et al. (2024) Multimedia and immersive training materials influence impressions of learning but not learning outcomes
finding: Richer VR training raised confidence in learning but not recognition-test performance.
numbers: Two experiments (video in VR vs static diagram; immersive VR vs static diagram); sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract page only. Humans, not LLMs.
agent_relevance: Another case where feeling and result split.
